Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A needles/medical visual trigger is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is clear trauma-related medical treatment, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in threat, memory, appraisals, or strategies. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal danger and intrusion rather than medical trauma cues, so this trigger appears clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid site of the event' is difficult to interpret coherently for ongoing or domestic partner abuse in this profile. If the abuse occurred in shared/home spaces, the profile would usually show corresponding location-specific triggers or avoidance themes; instead the threat items focus on general vigilance and home intrusion, making this item feel insufficiently anchored to the rest of the selected content.

vignette: Bao, a 24-year-old painter, sits rigidly in his chair, his hands clenched in his lap. He speaks of the last six months as if describing a foreign country he has unwillingly come to inhabit. The trauma occurred in the place that was once his sanctuary: the small, light-filled studio attached to his apartment. His then-partner, Kenji, had locked him in after a minor argument escalated. Bao remembers the sound of the deadbolt clicking, the sudden shift in Kenji’s eyes, and the terrifying uncertainty of what would come next. The ensuing physical assault is a blur of disjointed sensory snapshots. He has a crystal-clear memory of the smell of turpentine and the precise pattern of the wood grain on the floorboards where he was pinned, but he cannot recall how the argument ended or how he got out of the room. This confusing sequence of events haunts him, a film reel with crucial frames missing. These fragmented memories are not passive recollections; they are active ambushes. An unwanted thought of Kenji’s voice (a trigger) can instantly plunge him back into the studio, the memory so vivid he can feel the cold floor against his cheek, as if it is happening right now. Because the memory intrudes with such sensory force, elements from it have begun to contaminate his present; he now finds the smell of turpentine or the sight of dark wood flooring can unexpectedly trigger the same wave of panic. This reliving of the event (Memory) immediately activates his sense of profound danger (Threat). His heart will pound, and he will begin scanning the room for exits, even in his own familiar living space. The intense fear sparked by the memory reinforces his core belief that he is inadequate, a person who was too weak to prevent what happened. This deep-seated sense of personal failing (Negative Appraisals) is a constant undercurrent, whispering that the event occurred because of the sort of person he is. His life has become a complex map of avoidance and hypervigilance, governed by a pervasive sense of threat. This constant state of high alert feels, to Bao, like definitive proof of his own weakness, confirming the belief that he is fundamentally broken by what happened. The belief that he is fundamentally unsafe (Negative Appraisals) means he is constantly on high alert. This state of threat monitoring, in turn, generates its own triggers; he finds himself listening for the faint sound of footsteps outside his door or the jingle of keys, each noise a potential prelude to intrusion. Any unexpected delay—his current partner running ten minutes late from the grocery store—becomes proof that something terrible is happening. This persistent sense of danger keeps his mind close to the event, as if needing to review it to stay one step ahead of a similar attack, which makes it far more likely that fragmented images of the assault will surface. This feeling of imminent danger (Threat) often forces him into a state of paralysis; when he hears a sudden noise at night, he will freeze completely in his bed, a reaction that only deepens his self-appraisal as helpless and inadequate. These moments of freezing (Maladaptive Strategy) do nothing to resolve the threat, instead leaving him trapped with his thoughts, which inevitably drift back to fragmented images of the assault (Memory). The feedback loops are now tightly woven into the fabric of his days. A trigger, such as feeling watched while sketching in a public park, will not only activate his threat system but also his impulse to flee or shut down. He has stopped going to parks entirely. By never testing his fear, he has inadvertently confirmed it; his nervous system interprets the successful avoidance as proof that the park was, in fact, dangerous, leaving his underlying sense of threat not only intact but strengthened. This avoidance of situations that might bring on the feelings of being trapped (Maladaptive Strategies) has shrunk his world, reinforcing his belief that he no longer belongs anywhere. At night, he puts off going to sleep, terrified of the nightmares, a strategy that leaves him exhausted and only makes the intrusive memories more potent the next day. The very act of avoiding anything that reminds him of Kenji—a particular musician, a brand of tea, the colour green—serves as a constant reminder of the trauma, bringing forth unwanted thoughts (Triggers) and confirming his own sense of being permanently broken (Negative Appraisals). Bao sought therapy after an incident last week. His new partner, meaning only to be affectionate, came up behind him while he was painting and placed his hands on his shoulders. Bao froze instantly, dropping his brush. The terror in his eyes was unmistakable, and the ensuing silence was filled with a shame so profound he could barely speak. He realized then that his internal world of threat was beginning to poison the first safe relationship he had known since the assault. Because he is so convinced that danger is everywhere and that he is incapable of handling it, ordinary sounds he once would have ignored now snag his attention as potential threats. He came to therapy not just to escape the memories, but because of a desperate fear that if he cannot change, he will lose the very connection that makes him feel he might one day belong somewhere again.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not demonstrate how the patient's negative beliefs cause him to develop or perceive new triggers.
The vignette does not demonstrate how the trauma memory itself causes new things to become triggers.
The vignette does not demonstrate how a general feeling of threat causes the trauma memory to surface.
The vignette does not demonstrate how the patient's maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance) lead to an increased sense of threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not demonstrate how the patient's negative beliefs cause him to develop or perceive new triggers.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not demonstrate how the trauma memory itself causes new things to become triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette does not demonstrate how a general feeling of threat causes the trauma memory to surface.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Threat: The vignette does not demonstrate how the patient's maladaptive strategies (e.g., avoidance) lead to an increased sense of threat.
  e.g. "Never having stayed in a situation long enough to find out it was safe, her body had never received the evidence it needed — the threat remained as high as the day it was set."
  e.g. "The checking and the avoidance had kept her alive, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing."
  e.g. "Without ever testing the feeling, she had no way to know that the threat was not what her body insisted it was — the safety behaviours had sealed that possibility off."
